Inside Big Tech companies' big slump this week

Oct 30, 2026
Inside Big Tech companies' big slump this week
Intel saw its stock plummet at historic rates on Friday, along with smaller drops from Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon.
Markets/Wall Streetby Caleigh Wells
Download
Intel's stock closed Friday down 28.58%. It's the worst the company has done on the stock market in half a century.
Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images
It was a bad week for Big Tech
Google’s parent company, Alphabet, lost $500 billion in stock value on Thursday following a rough third quarter earnings report.
On Friday, more tech giants joined the fray: Meta reported a negative free cash flow, and its stock dropped, along with Microsoft and Amazon. Intel fell the most, down 28.58% at the close of the market on Friday. It was Intel’s worst day on the stock market since 1974.
What struck Daniel Newman, CEO of the Futurum Group, was just how fast these companies took a turn for the worse.
“Monday, Tuesday, everyone was smiling,” he said. “Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, everybody was crying.”
Newman said that all these companies invest a lot in AI — but that wasn’t the problem.
“SpaceX, Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, all actually performed extremely well inside their cloud businesses,” he said, “but interestingly enough, we started to see some cracks inside other parts of the businesses.”
Google’s ad revenue isn’t working as well. Amazon’s e-commerce is seeing stubbornly slow growth. Microsoft is selling bonds to bankroll its spending. Intel isn’t selling enough PC components.
“They're kind of reaching their limits of being able to finance their growth,” said Peter Cohan, a management professor at Babson College. “And investors are getting impatient for a payoff.”
Cohan said that tech companies have been using their legacy businesses to pay for all their AI investment for a while and promising a big payout.
“There's a lot of jitters about how much money people are spending, companies are spending on AI capital expenditures, and not necessarily generating a clear return on investment,” he said.
At first blush, it looks similar to the dot-com bubble: Companies invested a lot, then failed to meet expectations, then said it would pay off — and then, it didn’t pay off.
“This time around, we're not seeing that,” said Matt Bryson, managing director of equity research at Wedbush Securities.
Bryson said that back then, the demand for more tech started to soften. That’s not what is happening now.
“No one is halting spend or slowing spend,” Bryson said. “The problem is, people keep on spending more and keep on telling investors that they're going to spend more.”
And with endless demand for more AI, the tech companies just keep looking for more ways to up their supply.
An AI bubble?

articles.title: Why companies offer buyouts versus layoffs
articles.text:
What are the advantages to buyouts versus layoffs?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 30, 2026
Why companies offer buyouts versus layoffs
Voluntary departures carry a reputational advantage over forced layoffs, shifting responsibility to employees who opt in.
Workplace/Jobsby Kristin Schwab
Download
Offering buyouts could show companies expect headwinds, and are planning ahead.
Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images
Microsoft announced earlier this week that it’s offering buyouts to 60,000 employees — about a quarter of its workforce. The company is looking to cut costs and offset investments in AI. Skydance is also making voluntary layoffs.
When comapnies offer buyouts, there are pros and cons compared to traditional layoffs.
In the late 1990s, during the dot-com bubble, Nita Chhinzer was working for a major telecommunications company that went through multiple rounds of voluntary layoffs.
“I would keep putting my hand up and I was like, ‘Can I please get the layoff?’” she said. The timing was right; she wanted to go back to school. “I did not get selected until I was finally in a small office where there was only four of us physically there in a section that held 160 people,” she said. (Yeah, the vibes were … weird.)
Nowadays, Chhinzer is a professor of organizational management at the University of Guelph near Toronto. She said when voluntary layoffs are executed thoughtfully, everyone feels a little less bad.
“If we allow people to opt in it’s almost like we’re shifting the responsibility, saying, ‘we didn’t pick you, you picked to be unemployed,’” Chhinzer said.
Letting employees choose their fate, though, comes with some risks.
“If you offer it, you give up a little bit of control over who’s taking it. Those who can actually go out and find something else to do might be more inclined to take those buyouts,” said Anthony Nyberg, a management professor at the University of South Carolina.
Top talent tends to leave, especially if they think more cuts are coming.
Investors prefer forced layoffs — they like to see more immediate and measurable savings. But Nyberg said those regular layoffs can cost more in the end.
“Layoffs are more likely to be followed by unintended turnover among your higher performers after the layoff,” he said.
Nita Chhinzer at the University of Guelph said she’s seen buyouts become the more popular choice in the last handful of years.
“So that tells me that companies are actually forecasting and looking forward six months or a year,” she said.
Chhinzer said firms are being more proactive about preparing for any storms — or planned investments — that are coming ahead.

articles.title: This measure of labor costs can signal when inflation's on the way
articles.text:
The cost of employing a worker rose .8% in Q3. What's that mean for inflation?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 30, 2026
This measure of labor costs can signal when inflation's on the way
The Employment Cost Index measures how much it costs to employ the average worker.
Workplace/Jobsby Nancy Marshall-Genzer
Download
The Employment Cost Index can predict future inflation, as employers may pass on higher costs to customers.
gorodenkoff/Getty Images
The cost of employing a worker rose 0.8% during the third quarter of this year, according to the seasonally adjusted Employment Cost Index released Friday morning by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That’s down from 0.9% in Q2.
Odds are you’ve never heard of this particular economic indicator, but the ECI tells us a lot about how companies are compensating their workers and, in turn, something about the broader economy.
The Employment Cost Index measures the average cost of having an employee.
The index comes out quarterly, said Ryan Nunn, a labor economist at the Yale Budget Lab. It’s based on a survey of businesses, “and we’re getting information about total compensation and not just wages.”
So that includes the cost of benefits: paid time off, health insurance, a 401(k). The Employment Cost Index can give economists a heads up about a problem that’s been plaguing this economy, said Tuan Nguyen, an economist at RSM.
”The Employment Cost Index is a very important leading indicator for inflation,” he said.
Dig into some economic data explainers
From August 2026: The Fed's preferred measure of inflation is changing
From July 2026: Why labor force participation has been trending lower for years
From March 2026: Despite revisions, labor productivity is still A-OK
From September 2025: Why trustworthy data is so important to everyone in the U.S. economy
From December 2024: What unit labor costs can tell us about where inflation is headed
Nguyen said the index can predict inflation three, six, or even 12 months down the road, because employers might pass higher labor costs on to their customers by raising prices. And if workers earn more, they tend to spend more, which pushes up demand and can also lead to even higher prices.
The Federal Reserve may be paying extra attention to the ECI now, said Allison Schrager, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute.
“The economy is just kind of weird right now,“ she said. “We have booms in some areas, slowdowns in others.”
Schrager sees the Employment Cost Index as a bright beacon in an ocean of uncertainty, even though it doesn’t make the headlines.

articles.title: Unemployment numbers are near a 57-year low. Why doesn't it feel like it?
articles.text:
Unemployment numbers look great. People don't feel the same
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 29, 2026
Unemployment numbers are near a 57-year low. Why doesn't it feel like it?
In a low-hire, low-fire job market, employment data and personal perceptions of the economy can tell different stories.
Workplace/Jobsby Kai Ryssdal and Sarah Leeson
Download
Weekly jobless claims are near record-low numbers. That doesn't mean everyone feels good, though.
Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
On a numbers level, the U.S. economy is strong. On Thursday, GDP came in at a healthy 3.4%, and the U.S. Department of Labor reported weekly jobless claims of 194,000 — that figure is near a 57-year low.
At the same time, numbers don't always translate to how people feel about the economy.
Tara Sinclair, chair of the economics department at George Washington University, joined “Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal, to talk about the truth behind the headline numbers. An edited transcript of their conversation is below.
Kai Ryssdal: So my executive producer and I were talking this morning, and she said to me, "You know, if I went outside and stopped 10 people on the street and told them about the data, [that] GDP is growing, [the] job market — while, you know, weird — is reasonably strong, they would look at me like I had three heads." And I guess that's the question I throw to you: What is going on?
Tara Sinclair: It is a wild time in the labor market because, on the one hand, as you point out, from many vantage points, the data look good. The claims, the data this morning, continue to be remarkably low. The unemployment rate remains historically low. Layoffs — despite the news about layoffs — also really low. But then, if you look at people trying to find a new job or thinking about changing jobs in order to get a higher wage, those numbers aren't looking so good, and that's probably what people are feeling.
Ryssdal: Do you suppose this lasts? I mean, it does seem we've been saying low-hire, low-fire for a very long time, and I guess I wonder what you think the short-, medium-term issue is.
Sinclair: Honestly, in many ways, I am somewhat heartened by its persistence, because for a while there, I thought that with the layoffs being low, but hires also being low, that the next step might be the shoe drops and layoffs go up. But we haven't seen that, and so it's kind of the better scenario there. But we'd really like to see an even better economy where firms feel comfortable hiring and people are changing jobs and getting raises and things like that.
Ryssdal: Right. So the labor market, meh — you know, nominally fine — but meh, really in perceived reality. I want you to answer this next question without using the word inflation. Other than the labor market, why are people so cranky out there?
Sinclair: Ooh, without saying the word inflation?
Ryssdal: Without using the word inflation or rising prices.
Sinclair: What about affordability or purchasing power?
Ryssdal: OK, all right, you can do that.
Sinclair: Well, if you think about it, people are looking at their wages, and it's just not keeping up. It's not allowing them to have the the lifestyle that they are used to having, that they were expecting to have at this stage in their lives. That's both an inflation story, but also a wages story.
Ryssdal: You used the word. You realize that, right?
Sinclair: I know, I know. I couldn't help it.
Ryssdal: That's fine. We'll let you go. That actually brings me to Chairman Warsh yesterday and the Federal Reserve deciding not to do anything with interest rates, while at the same time saying, “Nudge, nudge, wink, wink, we're looking at December,” and I guess my question is, why are they waiting? Clearly, they know inflation is elevated. He said it. What's the deal?
Sinclair: Well, there's a couple of reasons. First of all, we're really close to the midterms, and the Fed is trying to not rock the boat there. And on the other hand, they did raise rates last time, and so there's a sense in which they can let that kind of take hold a little bit before they give another dose of interest rate hikes because those are painful too. And so they don't want to do more than they have to.
Ryssdal: Let's bring it back to the labor market on the way out here. He seemed, and central bankers when they have been speaking, seem to be saying, “You know, the labor market's OK generally, and we really have to worry more about inflation.” You all right with that?
Sinclair: I think so because I don't think that the Fed has the ability to affect some of these underlying issues in the labor market. They're really targeting those top line numbers, which look pretty good.

Tales from a ghost tour company in the Big Easy
It gets especially busy during spooky season …
What’s That Like?by Emma Condon
Download
There's a whole economy behind the horror industry, and it comes alive at night (and around Halloween).
Mario Tama/Getty Images
Halloween is here, which means it’s that special time of year when people are on the hunt for a scare — something that will give them goosebumps and get the blood pumping.
Like any other Marketplace story, there is, of course, an economy behind all this: entire businesses dedicated to giving people a fright.
Few know this better than Kalila Smith. She’s the owner of Haunted History Tours in New Orleans, Louisiana. We spoke with her as a part of our ongoing series “What’s That Like?”, where we get to hear about all the weird and wonderful jobs that prop up our economy.
This time, we’re talking about ghost tours to help get you in the spooky spirit.
To hear about Smith’s business, click the play button at the top of the page.
